subject: math
title: Data and Graphs: Venn Diagrams, Pictographs, Bar Graphs and the Mode
seo_title: Grade 3 Data and Graphs Worksheets: Pictographs, Bar Graphs and Mode (Free, Answer Key, Ontario)
standard_text: Display sets of data, using many-to-one correspondence, in pictographs and bar graphs with proper sources, titles, and labels, and appropriate scales
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 math worksheets on data and graphs for the Ontario curriculum: Venn and Carroll diagrams, tally marks and frequency tables, pictographs with a key of 2, 5 or 10, bar graphs with scales of 2 and 5, and the mode. 100 EQAO-style questions with an answer key.
key_big: Read the key or the scale first. Then read every row or bar.
key_sub: If one symbol = 10, half a symbol = 5. A bar halfway between 6 and 8 shows 7. The mode is the answer that appears most often, not the biggest number. In a Venn diagram, count the overlap once.
body_html:
Sort, count, show, then explain

Data is information we collect, such as votes in a class survey. First we sort it. Then we count it with tally marks. Then we show it in a pictograph or a bar graph. Last, we say what the data tells us.

Venn and Carroll diagrams

A Venn diagram sorts things with circles. Things that fit both labels go in the overlap. Things that fit neither label go outside the circles. A Carroll diagram sorts things into boxes: each thing goes in the box for its row and its column.

Example

Where does 50 go?

50 is even. 50 is not more than 50.

Answer: Only in the Even circle

Tally marks and frequency tables

Draw one mark for each answer. The fifth mark goes across the other four. Count the groups by 5s, then add the single marks. The frequency is how many.

Pictographs

Look at the key first. In Grade 3, one symbol can stand for 2, 5 or 10. Count the symbols by 2s, 5s or 10s. Half a symbol stands for half of the key.

Example

How many students chose sledding?

2 circles. Count by 2s: 2, 4.

Answer: 4 students

Bar graphs

A good bar graph has a title, labels, a scale and a source (where the data came from). Find what the scale counts by: 2s or 5s. If a bar ends halfway between two lines, the number is halfway between them.

Example

How many more students chose hockey than skating?

Hockey 8, skating 5. 8 − 5 = 3.

Answer: 3 more students

The mode

The mode is the answer that appears most often. In a graph, it is the tallest bar or the longest row. In the graphs above, the mode is hockey.

Example

Goals in 6 games: 1, 3, 2, 3, 4, 3. What is the mode?

3 appears three times. No other number appears that often.

Answer: 3

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading each symbol as 1 (4 circles = 4)Use the key: 4 circles of 2 = 8
Saying half a symbol = 1 for every keyHalf a symbol is half of the key: half of 10 is 5
Reading a bar between lines as the lower lineHalfway between 6 and 8 is 7
Counting grid spaces instead of reading the scaleRead the number on the scale
Giving the biggest number as the modeThe mode is the answer that appears most often
Counting the overlap of a Venn diagram twiceCount each thing once

faq.q: What do Grade 3 students learn about data in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: They sort data in Venn and Carroll diagrams, organize it in frequency tables, show it in pictographs and bar graphs with a scale, find the mode, and explain what the data tells them.

faq.q: What is the mode in Grade 3 math?
faq.a: The mode is the value or answer that appears most often in a set of data. In 2, 3, 3, 5 the mode is 3; in a bar graph it is the category with the tallest bar.

faq.q: What is the difference between a Venn diagram and a Carroll diagram?
faq.a: A Venn diagram sorts things with overlapping circles, and things that fit both rules go in the overlap. A Carroll diagram sorts things into a grid of boxes, with one rule for the rows and one for the columns.

faq.q: Is data on the Grade 3 EQAO math assessment?
faq.a: Yes. The Grade 3 EQAO math assessment covers the strands of the Ontario curriculum, including Data, so students may read tables, pictographs and bar graphs and answer questions about them.

sets.title: Sort data in Venn and Carroll diagrams

items.q: How many numbers are even and more than 50?
items.e: Numbers that are in both circles go in the overlap, where the circles cross: 64, 90 and 58. That is 3 numbers. (7 counts the whole Even circle, and 6 counts the whole More than 50 circle.)

items.q: Where should 72 go?
items.e: 72 is even (it ends in 2) and 72 is more than 50. It belongs in both circles, so it goes in the overlap.

items.q: Where should 49 go?
items.e: 49 is odd (it ends in 9), so it is not in Even. 49 is less than 50, so it is not in More than 50. It goes outside both circles.

items.q: Where should 50 go?
items.e: 50 is even. But 50 is not more than 50, because it is equal to 50. So 50 goes only in the Even circle, not in the overlap.

items.q: One number is in the wrong place. Which number is it?
items.e: 46 is even, but 46 is less than 50. It should be only in the Even circle, not in the overlap. 64 is even and more than 50, so it is in the right place.

items.q: How many numbers are not even?
items.e: The numbers that are not even are outside the Even circle: 71, 85 and 53 in the other circle, and 27, 9 and 45 outside both circles. 3 + 3 = 6. Do not forget the numbers outside the circles.

items.q: How many students play both hockey and soccer?
items.e: Students who play both sports are in the overlap: Emma, Kai and Owen. That is 3 students.

items.q: How many students play hockey?
items.e: Count the whole hockey circle, including the overlap: Liam, Ava, Mateo, Chloe (4) and Emma, Kai, Owen (3). 4 + 3 = 7. (4 forgets the students in the overlap.)

items.q: How many students play neither hockey nor soccer?
items.e: Neither means outside both circles: Mei, Arjun, Zoe and Nathan. That is 4 students.

items.q: How many students were sorted altogether?
items.e: Count each student once: 4 + 3 + 2 + 4 = 13. Count the overlap only once, and remember the 4 students outside the circles. (9 forgets the students outside; 16 counts the overlap twice.)

items.q: Which box should 734 go in?
items.e: 734 ends in 4, so it is even: top row. 734 is 500 or more: right column. That is box B.

items.q: Which box should 815 go in?
items.e: 815 ends in 5, so it is odd: bottom row. 815 is 500 or more: right column. That is box D.

items.q: Which box should 500 go in?
items.e: 500 ends in 0, so it is even: top row. 500 is not less than 500, so it goes in the “500 or more” column. That is box B.

items.q: One number is in the wrong box. Which number is it?
items.e: 557 is odd, so the bottom row is right. But 557 is more than 500, so it belongs in the “500 or more” column, not “Less than 500”.

items.q: How many students have a pet and walk to school?
items.e: Find the box in the “Has a pet” row and the “Walks to school” column. It says 6.

items.q: How many students walk to school?
items.e: Add both boxes in the “Walks to school” column: 6 + 4 = 10. (6 is only the walkers with a pet.)

items.q: How many students do not have a pet?
items.e: Add both boxes in the “No pet” row: 4 + 7 = 11.

items.q: What is the best label for the second circle?
items.e: Every number in the second circle is in the 5 times table: 10, 20, 30, 15, 25, 35. It cannot be Odd numbers (10 is even) or Multiples of 10 (15 is not). More than 10 does not work, because 12 and 16 are outside it.

items.q: There are 28 students in the class. The numbers show how many students are in each part. How many students play neither sport?
items.e: Students in the circles: 10 + 5 + 6 = 21. 28 − 21 = 7 students are outside both circles. (2 comes from 28 − 15 − 11, which counts the 5 students in the overlap twice.)

items.q: Hana sorts the numbers 14, 30, 7 and 25 into a Venn diagram. The circles are “Even” and “Multiples of 5”. Which number goes in the overlap?
items.e: 30 is even and 30 is in the 5 times table, so it goes in the overlap. 25 is a multiple of 5 but odd. 14 is even but not a multiple of 5. 7 goes outside both circles.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 1 group of 5 and 3 more: 1 × 5 = 5, and 5 + 3 = 8.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 2 groups of 5 and 3 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 3 groups of 5 and 4 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 4 = 19.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 4 groups of 5 and 2 more: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 + 2 = 22.
16 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 1, so look for 3 groups of 5 and 1 single mark. That is C. A shows 21 (one group of 5 too many); B shows 15 (one single mark is missing); D shows 17 (one single mark too many).

items.q: What number should go in the Frequency column for Skating?
items.e: The frequency is the number the tally marks show. Skating has 2 groups of 5 and 4 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14.

items.q: Which sport got the most votes?
items.e: Skating has 14 votes (2 groups of 5 and 4 more). That is more than Sledding (11) and Hockey (9).

items.q: How many more students chose sledding than ringette?
items.e: Sledding 11, ringette 4. How many more means find the difference: 11 − 4 = 7.

items.q: How many students voted altogether? (Each student voted once.)
items.e: Find the Skating frequency first: 14. Then add all the rows: 9 + 14 + 6 + 11 + 4 = 44.

items.q: How many families have 4 people?
items.e: Find the row for 4 people. The frequency is 10 (2 groups of 5). The 4 is the number of people, not the number of families.

items.q: What is the most common family size?
items.e: The biggest frequency is 10, in the row for 4 people. So 4 people is the most common family size. 10 is how many families, not how many people.

items.q: How many families are in the survey?
items.e: Add the frequencies: 3 + 8 + 10 + 5 + 2 = 28 families. (20 is 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6, the family sizes.)

items.q: How many families have more than 4 people?
items.e: More than 4 means 5 or 6 people: 5 + 2 = 7 families. Do not include the families with exactly 4 people. (17 adds the 4-people row too.)

items.q: How many more chickadees than cardinals were seen?
items.e: Chickadee 12, cardinal 8. How many more means subtract: 12 − 8 = 4.

items.q: Which bird was seen half as many times as the chickadee?
items.e: The chickadee was seen 12 times. Half of 12 is 6. The blue jay has a frequency of 6.

items.q: Owen sees 4 more sparrows. What is the new frequency for Sparrow?
items.e: The sparrow frequency was 15. 4 more means add: 15 + 4 = 19.

items.q: Which survey question has answers that are numbers?
c: What is your favourite winter sport?
How do you get to school?
How many pets do you have?
items.e: “How many pets do you have?” has number answers, such as 0, 1, 2 or 3 (quantitative data). The other questions have answers that are words, such as red, bus or hockey (qualitative data).

items.q: Which survey question has answers that are words, not numbers?
c: How many people are in your family?
How many brothers and sisters do you have?
How many books did you read this week?
items.e: Favourite fruit gives answers like apple or banana. These are words (qualitative data). The other questions ask “how many”, so the answers are numbers.

items.q: Noah makes a tally of the Canada geese that fly over the schoolyard. He draws 4 groups of five and 3 single marks. How many geese has he counted?
items.e: Each group of five shows 5: 5, 10, 15, 20. Then 3 more: 21, 22, 23. So 23 geese. (Counting each group as 4 gives 19.)

items.q: Sofia counted 17 votes for ringette. How should she draw the tally?
items.e: 17 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 2. Draw 3 groups of five (four lines and one across) and 2 single marks. Never leave 5 or more single marks: make another group of five.

items.q: How many students chose ringette?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 2 students. The Ringette row has 7 circles: 7 × 2 = 14 students. (7 students would mean each circle is 1.)
Every star stands for the same number, so the row with the most stars shows the most. The Car row has 7 stars: 7 × 2 = 14 students.

items.q: How many apples did Zoe pick?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 2 apples. The Zoe row has 6 squares and half a square: 6 × 2 = 12, and half of 2 is 1, so 12 + 1 = 13 apples. (7 apples would mean each square is 1.)

items.q: Which row shows 3 books?
items.e: Half a circle is 1. The Arjun row has 1 circle and half a circle: 1 × 2 = 2, and half of 2 is 1, so 2 + 1 = 3 books.

items.q: Each star stands for 2 books. Priya read 14 books. How many stars should be in her row?
items.e: Count by 2s until you reach 14: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. That is 7 steps, so draw 7 stars. Check: 7 × 2 = 14. (Drawing 14 stars would mean each star stands for 1.)

items.q: How many more blue jays than juncos were seen?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 2 birds. Blue jay: 4 × 2 = 8. Junco: 1 × 2 = 2. How many more means find the difference: 8 − 2 = 6 birds. (3 is the difference in symbols, not in birds.)

items.q: Which row shows the fewest votes?
items.e: Every circle stands for the same number, so the row with the fewest circles shows the fewest. The Moose row has 1 circle: 1 × 2 = 2 votes.
Look at the key: each star stands for 5 laps. The Gr. 3 row has 2 stars: 2 × 5 = 10 laps. (2 laps would mean each star is 1.)

items.q: Which row shows 30 hot chocolates?
items.e: Each square = 5. 30 ÷ 5 = 6, so look for 6 squares. The Tue row has 6 squares: 6 × 5 = 30 hot chocolates.

items.q: Each square stands for 5 students. 30 students walk to school. How many squares should be in the Walk row?
items.e: Count by 5s until you reach 30: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. That is 6 steps, so draw 6 squares. Check: 6 × 5 = 30. (Drawing 30 squares would mean each square stands for 1.)
Look at the key: each star stands for 5 cans. The Mr. Chen row has 6 stars: 6 × 5 = 30 cans. (6 cans would mean each star is 1.)

items.q: How many more students ride a bike to school than take the bus?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 5 students. Bike: 4 × 5 = 20. Bus: 1 × 5 = 5. How many more means find the difference: 20 − 5 = 15 students. (3 is the difference in symbols, not in students.)

items.q: How many hot chocolates were sold altogether?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 5 hot chocolates. Read every row: Mon 5, Tue 35, Wed 25, Thu 30, Fri 10. Add them: 5 + 35 + 25 + 30 + 10 = 105 hot chocolates. (21 is the number of symbols.)
Look at the key: each star stands for 10 cans. The Mr. Khan row has 2 stars: 2 × 10 = 20 cans. (2 cans would mean each star is 1.)

items.q: How many laps did the Grade 2 students run?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 10 laps. The Gr. 2 row has 5 squares and half a square: 5 × 10 = 50, and half of 10 is 5, so 50 + 5 = 55 laps. (6 laps would mean each square is 1.)

items.q: In this pictograph, what does half a circle stand for?
items.e: The key says one whole circle = 10 apples. Half a circle is half of 10, which is 5 apples. (Half a symbol is not always 1. It is half of the key.)
Each star = 10. 60 ÷ 10 = 6, so look for 6 stars. The Wed row has 6 stars: 6 × 10 = 60 hot chocolates.

items.q: Each circle stands for 10 cans. Mr. Khan’s class collected 70 cans. How many circles should be in the class’s row?
items.e: Count by 10s until you reach 70: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70. That is 7 steps, so draw 7 circles. Check: 7 × 10 = 70. (Drawing 70 circles would mean each circle stands for 1.)

items.q: How many more apples did Emma pick than Noah?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 10 apples. Emma: 6 × 10 = 60. Noah: 4 × 10 = 40. How many more means find the difference: 60 − 40 = 20 apples. (2 is the difference in symbols, not in apples.)
Look at the key: each star stands for 10 cans. Read every row: Mr. Chen 60, Ms. Lee 30, Mme Roy 50, Mr. Khan 20. Add them: 60 + 30 + 50 + 20 = 160 cans. (16 is the number of symbols.)

sets.title: Bar graphs with scales of 2 and 5

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 2, 4, 6 … Each line is 2 more than the one before, so the scale counts by 2s. (Do not count the lines by 1s.)

items.q: How many cardinals were seen?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Cardinal ends on the line for 8. So the answer is 8 birds.

items.q: How many students chose skiing?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Skiing ends halfway between 12 and 14, so it shows 13. So the answer is 13 students.

items.q: Which bar shows 15 votes?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. Find 15 on the scale. The bar for Loon ends halfway between 14 and 16, so it shows 15.

items.q: How many students walk to school?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Walk ends halfway between 8 and 10, so it shows 9. So the answer is 9 students.

items.q: Which bar shows the fewest votes?
items.e: The bar for Beaver is the shortest one. The bar for Beaver ends on the line for 6. It shows 6 votes.

items.q: How many more books did Liam read than Priya?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. Liam: 15. Priya: 6. How many more means find the difference: 15 − 6 = 9 books.

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 5, 10, 15 … Each line is 5 more than the one before, so the scale counts by 5s. (Do not count the lines by 1s.)

items.q: How many laps did the Grade 5 students run?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. The bar for Gr. 5 ends on the line for 20. So the answer is 20 laps.

items.q: Which bar shows 30 apples?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. Find 30 on the scale. The bar for Mateo ends on the line for 30.

items.q: How many students chose sledding?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. The bar for Sledding ends on the line for 25. So the answer is 25 students.

items.q: Which bar shows the most hot chocolates?
items.e: The bar for Thu is the tallest one. The bar for Thu ends on the line for 30. It shows 30 hot chocolates.

items.q: How many more votes did the moose get than the polar bear?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. Moose: 25. Polar bear: 10. How many more means find the difference: 25 − 10 = 15 votes.

items.q: How many students come by car or take the bus to school?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. Car: 25. Bus: 35. Altogether means add: 25 + 35 = 60 students. (12 counts grid spaces, not students.)

items.q: Favourite Canadian animal (frequency table): Loon 8, Orca 13, Lynx 6, Bear 10. Which bar graph shows the same data?
items.e: C matches every number (the scale goes up by 2s). A: two bars are the wrong way round; B: a bar is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one bar is one line too high.

items.q: Hot chocolates sold at the rink (frequency table): Mon 25, Tue 35, Wed 15, Thu 30. Which bar graph shows the same data?
items.e: A matches every number (the scale goes up by 5s). B: two bars are the wrong way round; C: one bar is one line too high; D: one bar is one line too low.

items.q: Every bar graph needs a title, labels, a scale and a source. What is missing from this bar graph?
items.e: The graph has a scale (0, 2, 4 …), labels (Animal and Votes), and a source under the graph. It has no title at the top. A good title is “Favourite Canadian animal”.

items.q: Where did the data in this bar graph come from?
c: A vote in a Grade 3 class
items.e: The source is written under the graph: “Source: rink snack bar records”. The source tells where the data came from.

items.q: Owen will make a bar graph of this data: 15, 40, 25 and 35. Which scale is best?
items.e: All the numbers are in the 5 times table, so every bar ends on a line when the scale counts by 5s: 0, 5, 10 … 40. Counting by 1s or 2s needs too many lines (and 15, 25, 35 fall between lines of 2). Counting by 100s makes every bar too short to read.

items.q: Which list matches this bar graph? The numbers are in this order: Ms. Lee, Mr. Khan, Mme Roy, Mr. Chen.
items.e: The scale counts by 5s. The bar for Ms. Lee ends on the line for 30. The bar for Mr. Khan ends on the line for 45. The bar for Mme Roy ends on the line for 20. The bar for Mr. Chen ends on the line for 35. Counting grid spaces instead of reading the scale gives 6, 9, 4, 7.

items.q: What is the mode of this data?
items.e: The mode is the answer that was chosen most often. The tallest bar is Hockey, so the mode is hockey. 12 is how many students chose hockey. It is not the mode.

items.q: How many students chose hockey or skating?
items.e: The scale counts by 2s. Hockey ends on 12. Skating ends halfway between 8 and 10, so 9. Hockey or skating means add: 12 + 9 = 21. (Reading skating as 8 gives 20.)

items.q: How many more students chose sledding than skiing?
items.e: Sledding 10, skiing 6. How many more means subtract: 10 − 6 = 4. (16 is the sum, and 2 counts the grid spaces between the bars.)

items.q: Every Grade 3 student voted once. How many students voted?
items.e: Read every bar: 12, 9, 6, 10 and 5. Skating and ringette end between gridlines, so they are 9 and 5. 12 + 9 + 6 + 10 + 5 = 42. (Reading 9 and 5 as 8 and 4 gives 40.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: Ringette was the most popular sport.
Hockey got twice as many votes as sledding.
Skiing got more votes than skating.
Sledding got 1 more vote than skating.
items.e: Sledding 10 and skating 9: 10 − 9 = 1, so this is true. Skiing (6) is less than skating (9). Ringette (5) is the least popular. Twice sledding would be 20, not 12.

items.q: The gym teacher will plan activities for the two most popular sports. Which two?
items.e: The two tallest bars are hockey (12) and sledding (10). Skating is 9, just below sledding.

items.q: Which way to get to school is the mode?
items.e: The mode is the most common answer. The Bus row has the most squares (8 squares × 5 = 40 students), so the mode is bus. 40 and 8 are numbers of students and squares, not the mode.

items.q: How many students take the bus or come by car?
items.e: Each square = 5 students. Bus: 8 × 5 = 40. Car: 5 × 5 = 25. 40 + 25 = 65. (13 counts the squares, as if each square were 1.)

items.q: How many more students take the bus than walk?
items.e: Bus: 8 squares = 40. Walk: 7 squares = 35. 40 − 35 = 5. (1 is the difference in squares.)

items.q: The school wants fewer cars at drop-off. If 10 of the car students start to walk, how many students will walk?
items.e: Walk now: 7 squares × 5 = 35. 10 more students will walk: 35 + 10 = 45. (17 is 7 squares + 10, which reads each square as 1.)

items.q: Kai wrote down how many goals he scored in his last 7 hockey games: 2, 3, 1, 3, 5, 3, 2. What is the mode?
items.e: The mode is the number that appears most often. 3 appears three times, 2 appears twice, and 1 and 5 appear once. The mode is 3. (5 is the biggest number, not the mode.)

items.q: At drop-off, Zoe counted the people in each car: 2, 4, 1, 2, 3, 2, 5, 2. What is the mode?
items.e: 2 appears four times, more than any other number, so the mode is 2. (5 is the biggest number, and 4 is how many times 2 appears.)

items.q: Which set of data has a mode of 4?
items.e: In 4, 6, 4, 2, 4 the number 4 appears three times, so the mode is 4. The other modes are 6 (in 2, 4, 6, 6, 3), 1 (in 1, 4, 3, 1, 5) and 8 (in 9, 8, 4, 8, 7).

items.q: What is the mode of this data?
items.e: The mode is the dessert with the biggest frequency. Pumpkin pie has 11 votes, the most. 11 is the frequency, not the mode.

items.q: 4 more students vote for apple pie. What is the mode now?
items.e: Apple pie now has 8 + 4 = 12 votes. 12 is more than 11 (pumpkin pie), so apple pie is the new mode.

items.q: How much money did the four classes raise altogether?
items.e: The scale counts by 5s. Ms. Lee $35, Mr. Khan $50, Mme Roy $45, Mr. Chen $20. 35 + 50 + 45 + 20 = 150. (30 counts the grid spaces: 7 + 10 + 9 + 4.)

items.q: Next year, Mme Roy’s class wants to raise $60. How much more is that than this year?
items.e: Mme Roy’s bar ends on 45. 60 − 45 = 15, so $15 more. (Reading the bar as 40 gives $20; $105 adds instead of subtracting; $25 uses Ms. Lee’s bar, 35, by mistake.)

items.q: How many more chickadees were seen than blue jays and cardinals together?
items.e: Each circle = 2 birds, so half a circle = 1. Blue jay 2 × 2 + 1 = 5. Cardinal 3 × 2 = 6. Step 1: 5 + 6 = 11. Step 2: chickadee 7 × 2 = 14, and 14 − 11 = 3.

items.q: How many birds were seen altogether?
items.e: Chickadee 14, blue jay 5, cardinal 6, sparrow 9, junco 8. 14 + 5 + 6 + 9 + 8 = 42. (22 counts the circles. Leaving out the half circles gives 40.)

items.q: Arjun says, “Hockey is the favourite winter sport of every Grade 3 student in Canada.” Is he right?
c: No. Skating has the tallest bar.
Yes. Hockey has the tallest bar.
No. The data is from one school only.
items.e: The source says the data is from a vote of the Grade 3 classes at one school. It tells us about these students, not every Grade 3 student in Canada. Even at this school, most students did not choose hockey: 12 out of 42.
